h1: Primary and secondary sales in spirits
title: Primary and Secondary Sales in Spirits | Craft Beer School
desc: What primary, secondary and tertiary sales mean in Indian spirits, who records each one and why the numbers rarely agree in the same month.
teaser: Your company booked the sale. The bottle has not been drunk yet. That gap has a name.
standfirst: New joiners in spirits companies hear primary and secondary sales in their first meeting and rarely get a definition. Here is what each term counts, where the data comes from and how to read them together.
sections:
A bottle of whisky usually changes hands three times between the bottling hall and the glass.

  • Primary sales: the producer sells to the first buyer in the chain. In India that is a state government corporation in some states and a licensed wholesaler or distributor in others.
  • Secondary sales: the wholesaler or corporation sells to retail shops, bars, hotels and restaurants.
  • Tertiary sales: the shop sells to the consumer, or the bar pours the drink.

Primary sales are what the company invoices, so they drive revenue, excise payments and the finance team's month end. Secondary sales are closer to real demand. Tertiary sales are what the brand team really wants to know. They are also the hardest to see.
Why the trade in India has an extra layer of rules

Alcohol for human consumption sits outside GST in India and is largely a state subject. Each state sets its own excise duty, licences, price approvals and route to market. Stock moves under permits issued by the state excise department. Moving stock from one state to another needs export and import permits from both sides.

So a primary sale is not just an invoice. It is an invoice plus an excise permit, often a transport pass with a validity period plus duty that has either been paid or is held under bond. Rules and fees vary by state and change, so teams should work from the current notification in each state. Our guide to excise and state permits covers the process.
What a primary sale looks like from the plant

From the production floor, a primary sale is a truck leaving the bonded warehouse. Before it leaves, the cases have been bottled at a declared strength, commonly 42.8% ABV for mainstream Indian whisky (25 under proof, or 75 degrees proof on the old British scale), labelled for a specific state and checked against the permit. A truck of 750 ml bottles carries a set number of nine litre cases, the trade's standard unit of twelve bottles.

That is why primary sales come in lumps. A plant ships full trucks against permits, not a smooth daily flow. A single delayed permit can move hundreds of cases from one month into the next without any change in what people are drinking.
Secondary sales and the stock in between

The difference between primary and secondary sales over a period is the change in stock held by the wholesaler. Ship 5,000 cases into a state in a month while the wholesaler sells 4,200 to retail and channel stock rises by 800 cases.

Planners usually express channel stock as days or weeks of cover. If secondary sales run at 1,000 cases a week, 4,000 cases of stock is four weeks of cover. Too little means empty shelves during a festival. Too much means the distributor's cash is tied up, older stock sits in hot warehouses and the next primary order shrinks.

In the United States the same idea is called shipments and depletions. The vocabulary changes; the arithmetic does not.
Why the numbers disagree in the same month

Expect primary and secondary sales to diverge for reasons that have nothing to do with drinkers.

  1. Price or tax changes. The trade buys ahead of an increase or waits out a decrease.
  2. Financial year end. Pressure to close the year in March can lift primary sales while secondary sales stay flat.
  3. Launches. A new SKU needs stock on shelves before the first sale, so primary leads secondary for months.
  4. Permit timing. Delays in approvals shift trucks between periods.
  5. Seasonality. The trade stocks up before festive and wedding seasons.

None of these change the volume of whisky people drink. All of them change the dashboard.
Tertiary sales, the number everyone wants

True consumer sales are patchy in Indian spirits. Where the state runs retail, shop level data may or may not reach the producer. Where retail is private, coverage depends on retail audit panels, sales team visits and whatever the retailer chooses to share. Bars and restaurants are harder still.

Most teams therefore use secondary sales as their demand signal, cross-checked with retail audits and field reports. That is a reasonable compromise as long as everyone knows which number is on the slide.
A first check for your next review

Before your next monthly review, put primary and secondary sales for one state side by side for the last twelve months, both in nine litre equivalent cases. Add a third line for the running difference, which is channel stock. If that line keeps climbing, the brand is selling to the trade faster than the trade is selling to drinkers. That is the conversation to have before the next price increase, not after it.

For the money side of the same flow, our guide to whisky for finance new joiners is the next read.
faqs: What is the difference between primary and secondary sales?
Primary sales are from the producer to the first buyer, such as a state corporation or wholesaler. Secondary sales are from that buyer to retailers, bars and restaurants.
Secondary sales are the usual demand signal because they are closer to the consumer. Tertiary sales to the drinker are better still but rarely complete in India.
Why do primary sales come in lumps?
Spirits move in full trucks against state excise permits. A delayed permit or a year end push can shift hundreds of cases between months.
